title: Advanced Query Features
description: Reshape data with PIVOT, join to functions with CROSS APPLY, compute values with computed columns and sequences, and manage large datasets with partitioning.

data.text: Beyond the basics of SELECT, WHERE, and JOIN, SQL Server offers powerful features for reshaping data, computing values on the fly, generating unique numbers, and managing very large tables. This lesson covers the most useful ones.

PIVOT takes unique values from one column and turns them into multiple columns in the output — a crosstab. You provide an aggregate function (COUNT, SUM, etc.) and the column whose values become headers.

data.title: PIVOT example — products per category
data.code:
SELECT * FROM
(
    SELECT c.category_name, p.product_id
    FROM   production.products p
    INNER JOIN production.categories c
        ON c.category_id = p.category_id
) AS t
PIVOT(
    COUNT(product_id)
    FOR category_name IN
        ([Mountain Bikes], [Road Bikes], [Electric Bikes])
) AS pivot_table;

data.title: UNPIVOT is the reverse
data.text: Just as PIVOT turns rows into columns, UNPIVOT turns columns back into rows. Use it when you receive data in a crosstab format and need to normalize it for further processing.
CROSS APPLY — join to a table-valued function

CROSS APPLY works like INNER JOIN but with a table-valued function or a correlated subquery on the right side. For each row on the left, it executes the function and joins the result — useful for 'top N per group' queries.

data.title: Top products per category using CROSS APPLY
data.code:
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.GetTopProductsByCategory (@catId INT)
RETURNS TABLE
AS
RETURN (
    SELECT TOP 2 product_name, list_price
    FROM   production.products
    WHERE  category_id = @catId
    ORDER BY list_price DESC
);

SELECT
    c.category_name,
    p.product_name,
    p.list_price
FROM   production.categories c
CROSS APPLY dbo.GetTopProductsByCategory(c.category_id) p
ORDER BY c.category_name, p.list_price DESC;

data.title: OUTER APPLY keeps everything
data.text: CROSS APPLY is an INNER JOIN — rows with no match in the function are dropped. OUTER APPLY keeps them, with NULLs in the function's columns. Choose based on whether you want unmatched left rows.
A computed column is a virtual column whose value is derived from an expression over other columns. It saves you from repeating the same calculation in every query.

data.title: Add a persisted computed column
data.code:
ALTER TABLE persons
ADD full_name AS (first_name + ' ' + last_name) PERSISTED;

data.title: Persisted computed columns
data.text: A PERSISTED computed column stores the computed value on disk — it is recalculated on every write. You can only persist deterministic expressions (no GETDATE(), RAND(), etc.). Persisted computed columns can be indexed.
A SEQUENCE is a user-defined object that generates a series of numeric values. Unlike IDENTITY, a sequence is not tied to a table — the same sequence can feed IDs across multiple tables.

data.title: CREATE SEQUENCE and NEXT VALUE FOR
data.code:
CREATE SEQUENCE order_number
    AS INT
    START WITH 1
    INCREMENT BY 1;

data.title: Using a sequence in inserts
data.code:
INSERT INTO procurement.purchase_orders (order_id, vendor_id, order_date)
VALUES (NEXT VALUE FOR procurement.order_number, 1, '2019-05-01');

data.text: Partitioning splits a large table or index into smaller, more manageable pieces (partitions) based on a key — often a date column. Each partition can be stored on a different filegroup, backed up independently, and queried with partition elimination.

data.title: Create a partition function and scheme
Create a partitioned table
When partitioning helps
data.text: Partitioning shines on very large tables (hundreds of millions of rows+) — it enables partition switching (instant archive), parallel loading, and targeted backups. For smaller tables it adds overhead with no benefit.

A database snapshot is a read-only, transactionally consistent view of a database at a point in time. It uses a copy-on-write mechanism — pages are copied only when they change, so snapshots are space-efficient for incremental backups and reporting.

data.title: Create a database snapshot
data.code:
CREATE DATABASE HR_snapshot
ON (NAME = HR, FILENAME = 'D:\backup\HR_snapshot.ss')

data.title: Snapshot uses and caveats
data.text: Snapshots are great for reporting off a production database without blocking writes, and for quick rollback if a batch update goes wrong. But performance degrades as more pages diverge from the snapshot, and you cannot back up a snapshot.

data.title: Advanced query features
points: PIVOT rotates unique column values into headers; UNPIVOT reverses it
CROSS/OUTER APPLY joins a table to a table-valued function or correlated subquery — ideal for top-N-per-group
Computed columns encapsulate reusable expressions; PERSISTED stores them on disk (deterministic only)
SEQUENCE generates shared numeric values across multiple tables; IDENTITY is table-scoped only
Partitioning splits large tables by key for performance and manageability
Database snapshots provide read-only point-in-time views using copy-on-write
